related_questions.question: What causes your platelets to be low?

text_blocks.snippet: Low platelet counts, also known as thrombocytopenia, can stem from various factors, broadly categorized into issues with platelet production, destruction, or sequestration. Bone marrow disorders, certain medications, infections, autoimmune diseases, and even pregnancy can all contribute to this condition.
snippet_highlighted_words: Bone marrow disorders, certain medications, infections, autoimmune diseases, and even pregnancy

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at the causes:

list.title: Bone Marrow Disorders:
list.snippet: Conditions like aplastic anemia, myelodysplastic syndromes, and leukemia can affect the bone marrow's ability to produce platelets.

list.title: Cancer and Cancer Treatments:
list.snippet: Blood cancers (like leukemia and lymphoma) and treatments like chemotherapy and radiation can damage the bone marrow and hinder platelet production.

list.title: Nutrient Deficiencies:
list.snippet: Deficiencies in folate, vitamin B12, and other nutrients can impair platelet formation.

list.title: Infections:
list.snippet: Certain infections can directly affect the bone marrow or interfere with platelet production.

list.title: Autoimmune Diseases:
list.snippet: Conditions like lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, and immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) can cause the immune system to mistakenly attack and destroy platelets.

list.title: Infections:
list.snippet: Some infections can trigger an immune response that leads to platelet destruction.

list.title: Medications:
list.snippet: Certain medications, including some antibiotics, blood thinners, and other drugs, can cause increased platelet destruction.

list.title: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS):
list.snippet: This condition can damage red blood cells and reduce platelet counts.

list.title: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC):
list.snippet: This serious condition can cause widespread blood clotting and consumption of platelets.

list.title: Enlarged Spleen:
list.snippet: An enlarged spleen can trap platelets, reducing the number circulating in the bloodstream.

list.title: Distributional Thrombocytopenia:
list.snippet: This refers to low platelet counts caused by the spleen trapping a large proportion of platelets.

list.title: Pregnancy:
list.snippet: Some women develop mild thrombocytopenia during pregnancy, which usually resolves after delivery.

list.title: Alcohol Use Disorder:
list.snippet: Excessive alcohol consumption can impair platelet production and increase destruction.

list.title: Liver Cirrhosis:
list.snippet: Liver disease can lead to decreased platelet production and increased platelet destruction.

list.title: Major Blood Transfusions:
list.snippet: In rare cases, massive blood transfusions can lead to dilutional thrombocytopenia.

list.title: Sepsis:
list.snippet: Severe sepsis can cause both increased platelet destruction and impaired production.

related_questions.title: What to do to avoid bleeding?
list: Avoid strenuous activity, contact sports, lifting heavy objects, training to cough, forceful nose blowing, or constipation.
Avoid medications (see below) that affect blood clotting (unless approved by your doctor).
Do not take aspirin or any product that contains aspirin.
